options: If both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion
If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion

292.sol: Application of cytokinins to marketed vegetables can keep them fresh for several days. Shelf life of cut shoots and flowers is prolonged by employing the hormone cytokinin. The reason is that the cytokinin increases retention of chlorophyll and delayed senescence in leaves. Cytokinin as the name suggests, is essential for cell division or cytokinesis. It promotes cell division along with auxin by controlling the activity of cyclin dependent kinases.

Assertion : $E^{\circ}$ for $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+} / \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ is more positive than $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+} / \mathrm{Cr}^{2+}$.

If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion
If assertion is true, but reason is false
Both assertion and reason are false statements.
564.sol:
It is known that the value of $E^{{}^{\circ}}$ becomes more negative down the series. As the chromium is present below in electrochemical series than $\mathrm{Mn}$, so $\mathrm{Mn}$ has more positive $E^{{}^{\circ}}$ value than $\mathrm{Cr}$.

\begin{array}{ll}$\mathrm{Mn} \rightarrow$3 d⁵ 4 s²,  $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} \rightarrow$3 d⁵ 4 s⁰ \\
$\mathrm{Cr} \rightarrow$3 d⁵ 4 s¹,  $\mathrm{Cr}^{2+} \rightarrow$3 d⁴ 4 s⁰
\end{array}

For elimination of one electron from $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$, more energy is required due to its stable configuration. That is why third ionization energy of $\mathrm{Mn}$ is larger than $\mathrm{Cr}$.

5106.text: If \(0.5 $\mathrm{ mol}$\) of a metal forms hexagonal close packed structure, the total number of voids, and tetrahedral voids respectively in mol are

Number of moles of metal in close packed structure \(=0.5 \mathrm{ mol}\)
No. of atoms in 1 mole of mole \(=N_A\)
\(\therefore\) Number of atoms in \(0.5 \mathrm{ mol}\) of metal
\(=0.5 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}=3.011 \times 10^{23}\)
Also, number of tetrahedral voids \(=2 \times\) number of metal atoms in close packed structure
\(\therefore\) Number of tetrahadral voids \(=2 \times 3.011 \times 10^{23}\)
\(=6.022 \times 10^{23} \approx 1 \mathrm{ mol}\)
Number of octahedral void \(=\) number of metal atoms in close packed structure
So, that number of octahedral voids \(=3.011 \times 10^{23}\)
\(=0.5 \mathrm{ mol}\)
Total number of voids
$\begin{aligned}
&$=$\text{ tetrahedral void }+ \text{ octahedral void }\\
& =6.022 \times 10^{23}+3.011 \times 10^{23} \\
& =9.05 \times 10^{23} \approx 1.$5 $\mathrm{ mol}
\end{aligned}\)
Therefore, total number$ of $voids and tetrahedral voids in hexagonal close packed structure are \(1.5 \mathrm{ mol}\) and \(1.0 \mathrm{ mol}\) respectively. Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.$

10756.text: Nine balls one drawn simultaneously from a bad containing $5$ white and 7 black balls. The probability of drawing $3$ white and $6$black balls is
10756.sol:
Out of $12$ balls we have to draw $9$ balls.

Therefore, selecting $9$ balls from $12$ balls can be done in $n\left(S\right) = C9 12 \text{ways}$

$= \dfrac{12 !}{9 ! \times 3 !} = 220$

Now, number of ways for selecting $3$ white balls will be $= C3 5 = \dfrac{5 !}{3 ! \times 2 !} = 10$

Number of ways for selecting $6$ black balls will be $= C6 7 = \dfrac{7 !}{6 ! \times 1 !} = 7$

Therefore, total number of ways for selecting $3$ white and $6$ black balls$n\left(P\right) = 10 \times 7 = 70$

Therefore, probability of getting $3$ white and $6$ black balls$= \dfrac{n\left(P\right)}{n\left(S\right)} = \dfrac{70}{220} = \dfrac{7}{22}$

19877.subject: Chemistry
19877.text: $\mathrm{X} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Y}$ is a first order reaction where $1.0 \mathrm{ mol} / \mathrm{L}$ of the reactant yields $0.4 \mathrm{ mol} / \mathrm{L}$ of Y in 200 minutes. Calculate the half-life period of the reaction in minutes.
19877.sol:
The reaction is $\mathrm{X} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Y}$.

Let the initial concentration of $\mathrm{X}$ be $[A]_0 = 1.0 \text{ mol/L}$.

At time $t = 200 \text{ minutes}$, the concentration of $\mathrm{Y}$ formed is $0.4 \text{ mol/L}$.

From the stoichiometry, the amount of $\mathrm{X}$ consumed is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times [\mathrm{Y}] = \dfrac{0.4}{2} = 0.2 \text{ mol/L}$.

The concentration of $\mathrm{X}$ remaining at $t = 200 \text{ minutes}$ is $[A]_t = [A]_0 - 0.2 = 1.0 - 0.2 = 0.8 \text{ mol/L}$.

For a first order reaction, the rate constant $k$ is given by $k = \dfrac{2.303}{t} \log \left( \dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]_t} \right).

$k = $\dfrac{2.303}{200} \log \left( \dfrac{1.0}{0.8} \right) = \dfrac{2.303}{200} \log(1.25) $\approx $\dfrac{2.303 \times 0.0969}{200}$ \approx$0.001115 \text{ min}^{-1}.

The half-life period $ t_{1/2}$ is given by $t_{1/2} = $\dfrac{0.693}{k}.

$ t_{1/2} = $\dfrac{0.693}{0.001115} \approx621.5 \text{ minutes}.

Answer: 621.5$

20925.subject: Mathematics
20925.text: Quadrilateral PQRS is inscribed inside a rectangle of dimensions $10 \mathrm{ cm} \times 8 \mathrm{ cm}$. The value of ' $x$ ', if the area of the quadrilateral is minimum is
20925.sol:
Let the rectangle be $ABCD$ with $AB = CD = 10$ cm and $AD = BC = 8$ cm. Let $AQ = x$, $BR = x$, $CS = x$, and $DP = x$.

The points are located as follows: $Q$ is on $AB$ such that $AQ = x$, so $QB = 10 - x$. $R$ is on $BC$ such that $BR = x$, so $RC = 8 - x$. $S$ is on $CD$ such that $CS = x$, so $DS = 10 - x$. $P$ is on $AD$ such that $DP = x$, so $AP = 8 - x$.

The area of the quadrilateral $PQRS$ is the area of the rectangle $ABCD$ minus the sum of the areas of the four right-angled triangles at the corners: $\triangle APQ$, $\triangle BQR$, $\triangle CRS$, and $\triangle DSP$.

Area of $\triangle APQ = \dfrac{1}{2} \times AP \times AQ = \dfrac{1}{2}(8 - x)x = 4x - \dfrac{x^2}{2}$.
Area of $\triangle BQR = \dfrac{1}{2} \times BQ \times BR = \dfrac{1}{2}(10 - x)x = 5x - \dfrac{x^2}{2}$.
Area of $\triangle CRS = \dfrac{1}{2} \times RC \times CS = \dfrac{1}{2}(8 - x)x = 4x - \dfrac{x^2}{2}$.
Area of $\triangle DSP = \dfrac{1}{2} \times DS \times DP = \dfrac{1}{2}(10 - x)x = 5x - \dfrac{x^2}{2}$.

Sum of areas of the four triangles $= 2(4x - \dfrac{x^2}{2}) + 2(5x - \dfrac{x^2}{2}) = 8x - x^2 + 10x - x^2 = 18x - 2x^2$.

Area of $PQRS = 10 \times 8 - (18x - 2x^2) = 80 - 18x + 2x^2$.

To find the minimum area, differentiate with respect to $x$ and set to zero:
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(80 - 18x + 2x^2) = -18 + 4x = 0$.

$4x = 18 \Rightarrow x = 4.5$ cm.

Answer: 4.5 cm

21521.subject: Mathematics
21521.sol:
Let $I = \int \dfrac{2x}{(x^2+1)(x^2+2)^2} dx$.

Substitute $t = x^2$, then $dt = 2x dx$.

The integral becomes $I = \int \dfrac{dt}{(t+1)(t+2)^2}$.

Using partial fractions, let $\dfrac{1}{(t+1)(t+2)^2} = \dfrac{A}{t+1} + \dfrac{B}{t+2} + \dfrac{C}{(t+2)^2}$.

Multiplying by $(t+1)(t+2)^2$, we get $1 = A(t+2)^2 + B(t+1)(t+2) + C(t+1)$.

For $t = -1$, $1 = A(1)^2 \Rightarrow A = 1$.

For $t = -2$, $1 = C(-1) \Rightarrow C = -1$.

Comparing coefficients of $t^2$, $0 = A + B \Rightarrow B = -A = -1$.

Thus, $I = \int \left( \dfrac{1}{t+1} - \dfrac{1}{t+2} - \dfrac{1}{(t+2)^2} \right) dt$.

Integrating, $I = \ln|t+1| - \ln|t+2| - \left( -\dfrac{1}{t+2} \right) + c = \ln\left| \dfrac{t+1}{t+2} \right| + \dfrac{1}{t+2} + c$.

Substituting $t = x^2$ back, $I = \ln\left| \dfrac{x^2+1}{x^2+2} \right| + \dfrac{1}{x^2+2} + c$.

21828.subject: Mathematics
21828.text: In how many ways can the squares of a $4 \times 2$ grid (4 rows and 2 columns) be filled with the letters of the word 'SPHERE' such that each row contains at least one letter?
21828.sol:
The word 'SPHERE' consists of 6 letters, in which 'E' appears twice and the rest are distinct.

The given grid has 4 rows and 2 columns, making a total of 8 squares.

Since there are 6 letters to be placed in 8 squares, exactly 2 squares will remain empty.

The condition states that each row must contain at least one letter. This implies that no row can be completely empty.

A row is completely empty if and only if both of its squares are empty.

The total number of ways to choose 2 empty squares out of the 8 squares is ^{8}C_{2} = 28$.

The number of ways to choose 2 empty squares such that they belong to the same row is 4 (since there are 4 rows).

Therefore, the number of ways to choose the 6 squares such that no row is empty is 28 - 4 = 24$.

For each valid selection of 6 squares, the number of ways to arrange the 6 letters of the word 'SPHERE' is $\dfrac{6!}{2!} = 360$.

The total number of ways to fill the grid is $24 \times 360 = 8640$.

Answer: $8640$

21897.subject: Mathematics
21897.text: Let $A$ and $B$ be two events such that one of the two events must occur. Given that the chance of occurrence of $A$ is $\dfrac{2}{3}$ the chance of occurrence of $B$, then odds in favour of $B$ is
21897.sol:
Let $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ be the probabilities of events $A$ and $B$ respectively. Since one of the two events must occur, $P(A) + P(B) = 1$.

Given $P(A) = \dfrac{2}{3} P(B)$, substituting this into the sum equation:

$\dfrac{2}{3} P(B) + P(B) = 1$

$\dfrac{5}{3} P(B) = 1 \Rightarrow P(B) = \dfrac{3}{5}$.

Then $P(A) = 1 - \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{2}{5}$.

The odds in favour of $B$ are defined as the ratio of the probability of occurrence of $B$ to the probability of non-occurrence of $B$, which is $P(B) : P(B^{c})$.

$P(B^{c}) = 1 - P(B) = 1 - \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{2}{5}$.

Odds in favour of $B = \dfrac{3}{5} : \dfrac{2}{5} = 3 : 2$.

Answer: $3: 2$

23179.subject: Physics
23179.text: A copper and a steel wire of same diameter are connected end to end. A deforming force $F_1$ is applied to the wire which causes an elongation of $1 \mathrm{ cm}$. The two wires will have
23179.sol:
Let the copper wire have Young's modulus $Y_C$ and the steel wire have Young's modulus $Y_S$. Both wires have the same diameter, so they have the same cross-sectional area $A$.

When connected end to end and subjected to a deforming force $F_1$, the tension in both wires is the same, equal to $F_1$.

The stress in each wire is given by $\sigma = \dfrac{F_1}{A}$. Since $F_1$ and $A$ are the same for both wires, the stress is the same in both wires.

The strain in each wire is given by $\epsilon = \dfrac{\sigma}{Y}$. Since the Young's moduli $Y_C$ and $Y_S$ are different for copper and steel, the strains $\epsilon_C = \dfrac{F_1}{A Y_C}$ and $\epsilon_S = \dfrac{F_1}{A Y_S}$ will be different.

Therefore, the two wires will have different strains.

Answer: different strain

26521.text: Consider a configuration of $n$ identical units, each consisting of three layers. The first layer is a column of air of height $h = \dfrac{1}{3}cm$, and the second and third layers are of equal thickness $d = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{2}cm$, and refractive indices ${\mu}_{1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$ and ${\mu}_{2} = \sqrt{3}$, respectively. A light source $O$ is placed on the top of the first unit, as shown in the figure. A ray of light from $O$ is incident on the second layer of the first unit at an angle of $\theta = 60 °$ to the normal. For a specific value of $n$, the ray of light emerges from the bottom of the configuration at a distance $l = \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{3}}cm$, as shown in the figure. The value of $n$ is _______.
26521.sol:
Considering a single unit with three layers. The figure below shows the refraction of light as it moves from one medium to others.

For the first interface,

${x}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times tan60 ° = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}cm$

Using Snell's law,

${\mu}_{1}sin{\theta}_{1} = {\mu}_{2}sin{\theta}_{2}$

$⇒ 1 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}} \times sin{\theta}_{2}$

$⇒ {\theta}_{2} = 45 °$

For the second interface,

$⇒ {x}_{2} = d \times tan45 ° = d$

And again using Snell's law,

$\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}} \times sin45 = \sqrt{3} \times sin{\theta}_{3}$

$⇒ \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}} \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{3}sin{\theta}_{3}$

$⇒ {\theta}_{3} = 30 °$

$⇒ {x}_{3} = d \times tan30 ° = \dfrac{d}{\sqrt{3}}$

$∴ {x}_{1} + {x}_{2} + {x}_{3} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} + \dfrac{\left(\sqrt{3} - 1\right)}{2}\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$

$= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}cm$

$∴ n = \dfrac{1}{{x}_{1} + {x}_{2} + {x}_{3}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{3}}}{\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}} = 4$

Thus, the value of $n = 4$.

26730.text: As shown in the figure, a ray $AB$ of unpolarized light enters from water of refractive index $n_w = 4/3$ into a medium of refractive index $n_p = 4/\sqrt{3}$ after passing through a glass plate of refractive index $n_g = 1.5$ and a layer of water. At a particular incident angle $i$ the reflected ray $CD$ is polarized in the direction as shown in the figure. The value of $i$ (in degrees) is:
26730.sol:
Let the angle of incidence at the first interface (water to glass) be $i$.

By applying Snell's law at the successive parallel interfaces, we can find the angle of incidence at the interface where the reflection occurs (water to medium $n_p$).

For the first interface (water to glass):
$n_w \sin i = n_g \sin r_1$

For the second interface (glass to water):
$n_g \sin r_1 = n_w \sin r_2$

From the above two equations, we get:
$n_w \sin i = n_w \sin r_2 \implies r_2 = i$

Thus, the angle of incidence at the third interface (water to medium $n_p$) is also $i$.

The problem states that the reflected ray is completely polarized with its electric field perpendicular to the plane of incidence (indicated by the dots on ray $CD$). This complete polarization upon reflection occurs when the light is incident at Brewster's angle $\theta_B$.

According to Brewster's law for the interface between water and medium $n_p$:
$\tan \theta_B = \dfrac{n_p}{n_w}$

Since the angle of incidence at this interface is $i$, we have $i = \theta_B$. Substituting the given refractive indices:
$\tan i = \dfrac{4/\sqrt{3}}{4/3}$

$\tan i = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3}$

Therefore, the angle of incidence is:
$i = 60^\circ$

Answer: $60$

$x + 6(-2) = -4$

$x = +8$

Since the oxidation state of Xe is $+8$, all $8$ of its valence electrons are involved in bonding with the $6$ oxygen atoms. There are no non-bonding electrons left on the central atom.

Number of lone pairs on Xe $= 0$

Xe forms $6$ $\sigma$ bonds with the $6$ oxygen atoms (and $2$ $\pi$ bonds to satisfy its $+8$ oxidation state and minimize formal charge).

Number of $\sigma$ bond-pairs $= 6$

Total number of $\sigma$ bond-pairs and lone pairs around the central atom $= 6 + 0 = 6$.

Answer: $6$

31631.subject: Chemistry
31631.text:
Which of the following statements are not correct?
A. For water, magnitude of $K_b$ is more than the magnitude of $K_f$.
B. The elevation in boiling point of water when a non-volatile solute is added to it is larger in magnitude than its depression in freezing point.
C. Osmotic pressure measurement is preferred over any other colligative property to determine molar mass of proteins and polymers.
D. The dimerised form of benzoic acid in benzene is $C_6H_5-\underset{O}{\overset{O}{\|}}C-OH \cdots\cdots O=\underset{OH}{\overset{|}{C}}-C_6H_5$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
31631.sol:
For water, the molal elevation constant $K_b = 0.52 \text{ K kg mol}^{-1}$ and the molal depression constant $K_f = 1.86 \text{ K kg mol}^{-1}$. Thus, $K_b < K_f$. Statement A is incorrect.

For a solution with a given molality $m$ of a non-volatile solute, the elevation in boiling point is $\Delta T_b = K_b m$ and the depression in freezing point is $\Delta T_f = K_f m$. Since $K_b < K_f$, it follows that $\Delta T_b < \Delta T_f$. Statement B is incorrect.

Osmotic pressure measurement is preferred for determining the molar mass of macromolecules such as proteins and polymers because the measurement is done at room temperature and the magnitude of osmotic pressure is significant even for very dilute solutions. Statement C is correct.

In benzene, benzoic acid undergoes dimerization through intermolecular hydrogen bonding, forming a cyclic dimer with two hydrogen bonds. The structure given in statement D represents a linear association with only one hydrogen bond. Statement D is incorrect.

Therefore, statements A, B, and D are incorrect.

Answer: A, B and D only

32170.subject: Chemistry
32170.text: The work functions of two metals $\left(M_{A}\right.$ and $\left.M_{B}\right) are in the$1: 2$ ratio. When these metals are exposed to photons of energy 6 eV, the kinetic energy of liberated electrons of $M_{A}: M_{B}$ is in the ratio of $2.642: 1$. The work functions (in eV) of $M_{A} and M_{B}$ are respectively.$
32170.sol:
The work functions satisfy $W_A : W_B = 1:2$.
Let $W_A = W$ and $W_B = 2W$.
Using the photoelectric equation
$KE = h\nu - W$, we have $KE_A = 6 - W$ and $KE_B = 6 - 2W$.
Given the kinetic energy ratio $\frac{KE_A}{KE_B} = 2.642$, we get $\frac{6-W}{6-2W} = 2.642$.
Solving: $6 - W = 2.642(6 - 2W)$ gives $6 - W = 15.852 - 5.284W$
So $4.284W = 9.852$ and $W = 2.3$ eV.
Thus $W_A = 2.3$ eV and $W_B = 4.6$ eV.

32875.text: Let $l$ be a line which is normal to the curve $y = 2{x}^{2} + x + 2$ at a point $P$ on the curve. If the point $Q\left(6, 4\right)$ lies on the line $l$ and $O$ is origin, then the area of the triangle $OPQ$ is equal to _____.
32875.sol:
The given curve is $y = 2{x}^{2} + x + 2$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4x + 1$

Let $P$ be $\left(h, k\right)$, then normal at $P$ is

$y - k = - \dfrac{1}{4h + 1}\left(x - h\right)

Since this normal passes through $Q$\left(6, 4\right)$

$∴ 4 - k = - \dfrac{1}{4h + 1}\left(6 - h\right)

$⇒ $\left(4h + 1\right)\left(4 - k\right) + 6 - h = 0$

Also $k = 2{h}^{2} + h + 2$

$∴ \left(4h + 1\right)\left(4 - 2{h}^{2} - h - 2\right)$ + 6 + h = 0$

$⇒ 4{h}^{3} - 3{h}^{2} + 3h - 8 = 0$

$⇒ h = 1, k = 5$

So $P ≡ $\left(1, 5\right)$

Now area of $∆ OPQ$ will be $= \dfrac{1}{2}\left|\begin{cases}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 6 & 4\end{cases}$\right|$ = 13$

42052.subject: Physics
42052.text: Assume that a drop of a liquid evaporates by a decrease in its surface energy so that its temperature remains unchanged. The minimum radius of the drop for this to be possible is. (The surface tension is $T$, the density of the liquid is$ρ$ and $L$ is its latent heat of vaporisation.)
42052.sol:
Let the radius of the drop at time $t = t$ be $r$ and at an instant $t = t + dt$ be $r - dr$

As surface area is given by, $A = 4\pi{r}^{2}$,

$∴$ decrease in surface area is,

$dA = 4\pi\left(2rdr\right)$

$∴$ Decrease in surface energy during time $dt$ is,

$dU = TdA = T \cdot 8\pirdr . . . \left(1\right)$

Decrease in volume during time $dt$ is,

$dV = 4\pi{r}^{2}dr$

$∴$ Decrease in mass during time $dt$ is,

$dm = ρdV = 4\piρ{r}^{2}dr$

$∴$ Heat required in vaporisation is,

$dQ = Ldm = 4\piρ{r}^{2}drL . . . \left(2\right)$

Apply conservation of energy,

decrease in surface energy$=$heat required in vaporisation.

$⇒ dU = dQ$

$⇒ 8T\pirdr = 4\piρ{r}^{2}drL$

$⇒ 2T = ρrL$

$⇒ r = \dfrac{2T}{ρL}$

Hence, the minimum radius is $\dfrac{2T}{ρL}$

42979.text: The $X - Y$ plane be taken as the boundary between two transparent media ${M}_{1}$ and ${M}_{2}$. ${M}_{1}$ in $Z \ge 0$ has a refractive index of $\sqrt{2}$ and ${M}_{2}$ with $Z < 0$ has a refractive index of $\sqrt{3}$. A ray of light travelling in ${M}_{1}$ along the direction given by the vector $\overset{\to}{A} = 4\sqrt{3i} - 3\sqrt{3}j - 5\overset{^}{k}$, is incident on the plane of separation. The value of difference between the angle of incident in ${M}_{1}$ and the angle of refraction in ${M}_{2}$ will be _____ degree.
42979.sol:
Given: $\overset{\to}{A} = 4\sqrt{3i} - 3\sqrt{3j} - 5\overset{^}{k}$

As incident vector $A$ makes $i$ angle with normal $Z$-axis and refracted vector $R$ makes $r$ angle with normal $Z$- axis.

The angle made by the incident ray with the normal is given as

$i = \cos^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{{A}_{z}}{A}\right) = \cos^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{( 4\sqrt{3}{)}^{2} + ( 3\sqrt{3}{)}^{2} + {5}^{2}}}\right)$

$= \cos^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{5}{10}\right) ⇒ i = 60 °$

Applying Snell's law of refraction at the interface of two media

${\mu}_{1}sini = {\mu}_{2}sinr$

$⇒ \sqrt{2}sin60 ° = \sqrt{3} \times sinr$

$⇒ r = 45 °$

Difference between $i$ and $r$ $= 60 ° - 45 ° = 15 °$

43154.text: A particle is rotating in a circular path and at any instant its motion can be described as $\theta = \dfrac{5t^4}{40} - \dfrac{t^3}{3}$. The angular acceleration of the particle after $10$ seconds is _______ rad/s$^2$.
43154.sol:
Given $\theta = \dfrac{5t^4}{40} - \dfrac{t^3}{3} = \dfrac{t^4}{8} - \dfrac{t^3}{3}$

Angular velocity $\omega = \dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = \dfrac{4t^3}{8} - \dfrac{3t^2}{3} = \dfrac{t^3}{2} - t^2$

Angular acceleration $\alpha = \dfrac{d\omega}{dt} = \dfrac{3t^2}{2} - 2t$

At $t = 10$ s, $\alpha = \dfrac{3(10)^2}{2} - 2(10)$

$\alpha = 150 - 20 = 130$ rad/s$^2$

Answer: $130$

44272.text: Two beams of light having intensities $I$ and $4I$ interfere to produce a fringe pattern on a screen. The phase difference between the two beams are $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ at points $A$ and $B$ respectively. The difference between the resultant intensities at the two points is $xI$. The value of $x$ will be _____ .
44272.sol:
Given here, phase difference at point $A$ and $B$ are ${ϕ}_{A} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$and ${ϕ}_{B} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Resultant intensity at point $A$,

${I}_{A} = I + 4I + 2\sqrt{I}\sqrt{4I}cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

$⇒ {I}_{A} = 5I + 4I\left(0\right) = 5I$

Resultant intensity at point $B$,

${I}_{B} = I + 4I + 2\sqrt{I}\sqrt{4I}cos\left(60 °\right)$ $= 5I + 4I \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 7I$

Difference in intensities is ${I}_{B} - {I}_{A} = 7I - 5I = 2I$.

Thus, value of $x = 2$.

44530.sol:
Since the point $x=0$ is a node and reflection is taking place from point $x=0$. This means that reflection must be taking place from the fixed end and hence the reflected ray must suffer an additional phase change of $\pi$ or a path change of $\frac{\lambda}{2}$.
So, if $y_{\text{incident }}=a \cos (k x-\omega t) \begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow$y_${\text{incident }}$ & =a $\cos$(-k x-$\omega$t+$\pi)$\\
& =-a \cos ($\omega$t+k x)
\end{aligned}

Hence equation$ for $the other wave

y=a \cos (k x+$\omega$t+$\pi)$

49858.text:
During inelastic collision between two objects, which of the following quantity always remains
conserved?
49858.sol:
Since no external forces are acting on the colliding bodies during collision, thus total linear momentum is always conserved in all type of collisions but kinetic energy in not conserved in all collisions.

55780.subject: Chemistry
55780.text: The attractive interactions between cations and mobile electrons in metallic solid is called
55780.sol:
The attractive interactions between cations and mobile electrons define metallic bonding.

In metallic solids, metal atoms lose valence electrons to form cations, while delocalized electrons form a shared "sea" throughout the structure.

The electrostatic attraction between these positive metal ions and negative delocalized electrons constitutes the metallic bond, often described as the electron sea model.


Other bond types differ significantly: ionic bonding involves complete electron transfer between atoms, covalent bonding involves electron sharing between specific atoms, and weak dipole-dipole interactions occur between polar molecules rather than within metallic structures.


The correct classification is therefore $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

59391.subject: Chemistry
59391.text: How many moles of potassium chlorate are heated to produce $11 \cdot 2$ L oxygen at STP ?
59391.sol:
The balanced chemical equation for the decomposition of potassium chlorate is:

$2KClO_{3} \rightarrow 2KCl + 3O_{2}$

At STP, the volume of $1$ mole of an ideal gas is $22 \cdot 4$ L.

Number of moles of $O_{2}$ produced is:

$n(O_{2}) = \dfrac{11 \cdot 2}{22 \cdot 4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ mole

From the stoichiometry of the reaction, $3$ moles of $O_{2}$ are produced from $2$ moles of $KClO_{3}$.

Therefore, the number of moles of $KClO_{3}$ required to produce $\dfrac{1}{2}$ mole of $O_{2}$ is:

$n(KClO_{3}) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times n(O_{2}) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ mole

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{3}$ mole

62737.subject: Mathematics
62737.sol:
Evaluate the limit $L = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{(7^x - 1)^4}{\tan \left(\frac{x}{k}\right) \cdot \log \left(1 + \frac{x^2}{3}\right) \cdot \sin 4x}$ given that it equals $3(\log 7)^3$.

Apply standard limits $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{7^x - 1}{x} = \log 7$, $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\tan x}{x} = 1$, $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\log(1 + x)}{x} = 1$, and $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$.

Express each component in terms of these limits:
Numerator: $(7^x - 1)^4 = \left(\frac{7^x - 1}{x}\right)^4 x^4 \to (\log 7)^4 x^4$.
Denominator terms:
$\tan \left(\frac{x}{k}\right) = \frac{\tan(x/k)}{x/k} \cdot \frac{x}{k} \to \frac{x}{k}$,
$\log(1 + x^2/3) = \frac{\log(1 + x^2/3)}{x^2/3} \cdot \frac{x^2}{3} \to \frac{x^2}{3}$,
$\sin 4x = \frac{\sin 4x}{4x} \cdot 4x \to 4x$.

Substitute into $L$:
$L = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{(\log 7)^4 x^4}{(x/k)(x^2/3)(4x)} = \frac{(\log 7)^4 x^4}{(4x^4)/(3k)} = \frac{3k (\log 7)^4}{4}$.

Set equal to given value:
$\frac{3k (\log 7)^4}{4} = 3(\log 7)^3$.
Divide both sides by $3(\log 7)^3$: $\frac{k \log 7}{4} = 1$ so $k = \frac{4}{\log 7} = 4(\log 7)^{-1}$.

This matches option A.

63175.subject: Mathematics
63175.text: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}_{3 \times 3}$, and $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \gamma & -1 & 1 \\ \alpha & 6 & -5 \\ \beta & -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}_{3 \times 3}$, then $|\alpha \cdot \beta \cdot \gamma| = _____ (where $|\cdot|$ denotes the absolute value)$
63175.sol:
The determinant of matrix $A$ is:

$|A| = 2(1 \times 3 - 0 \times 1) - 0 + (-1)(5 \times 1 - 1 \times 0) = 6 - 5 = 1$

Since $|A| = 1$, the inverse of $A$ is simply its adjugate matrix, $A^{-1} = \text{adj}(A)$.

The elements $\gamma, \alpha, \beta$ form the first column of $A^{-1}$, which corresponds to the cofactors $C_{11}, C_{12}, C_{13}$ of the first row of matrix $A$.

Calculating these cofactors:

$C_{11} = (1)(3) - (0)(1) = 3 \Rightarrow \gamma = 3$

$C_{12} = -((5)(3) - (0)(0)) = -15 \Rightarrow \alpha = -15$

$C_{13} = (5)(1) - (1)(0) = 5 \Rightarrow \beta = 5$

The product of these values is:

$\alpha \cdot \beta \cdot \gamma = (-15) \cdot 5 \cdot 3 = -225$

Taking the absolute value:

$|\alpha \cdot \beta \cdot \gamma| = |-225| = 225$

Answer: $225$

64085.sol:
Let $\mathrm{f}(x)=x^3+x-1$
A root of $\mathrm{f}(x)$ exists, if $\mathrm{f}(x)=0$ for at least one value of $x$. $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{f}(0)=-1 < 0 \\ \text{$ and $} \mathrm{f}(1)=1>0
\end{aligned} \therefore \quad$ By intermediate value theorem, there has to be a point ' $c$ ' between 0 and 1 such that $\mathrm{f}(x)=0$.
$\therefore \quad$ The given equation has exactly one real root.
Alternate Method:
Let $\mathrm{f}(x)=x^3+x-1
$\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore \quad \mathrmf^{\prime}(x)=3 x²+1 \\
\quad \Rightarrow \mathrmf^{\prime}(x)>0 \quad \forall x \in $\mathrm{R}$
\end{array}$\Rightarrow \mathrm{f}(x)$ is an increasing function.
$\Rightarrow \mathrm{f}(x)$ intersects $\mathrm{X}$-axis at only one point.
$\therefore \quad$ The given equation has exactly one real root.

66587.subject: Physics
66587.text: The maximum velocity of the photoelectrons emitted by a metal surface is $9 \times 10^5 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$. The value of ratio of charge (e) to mass (m) of the photoelectron is $1.8 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{kg}$. The value of stopping potential in volt is
66587.sol:
The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is given by $KE_{\text\max} = \frac{1}{2}mv_{\text\max^2$ and also by $KE_{\text\max} = eV_s$, where $m$ is the mass of the electron, $v_{\text\max}$ is the maximum velocity, $e$ is the charge of the electron, and $V_s$ is the stopping potential.

Combining these equations provides $\frac{1}{2}mv_{\text\max^2 = eV_s$.

Solving for $V_s$ yields $V_s = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{m}{e} \cdot v_{\text\max^2$.

Given $\frac{e}{m} = 1.8 \times 10^{11} \, \text{C/kg}$, it follows that $\frac{m}{e} = \frac{1}{1.8 \times 10^{11}} \, \text{kg/C}$.

Substituting this and $v_{\text\max} = 9 \times 10^{5} \, \text{m/s}$ into the expression for $V_s$ gives

$V_s = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{1.8 \times 10^{11}} \cdot (9 \times 10^{5})^2$

which simplifies to

$V_s = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{81 \times 10^{10}}{1.8 \times 10^{11}} = \frac{81 \times 10^{10}}{3.6 \times 10^{11}} = \frac{81}{36} = 2.25 \, \text{V}$.

Stopping potential: $2.25 \, \text{V}$
(Answer choice B)

66760.text: In the circuit shown, when the current '$i$' is $3\text{A}$ and increasing at the rate of $1\text{A/s}$ the measurement of the potential difference between A and B is $12\ \text{V}$. But when the same current $3\text{A}$ is decreasing at the rate of $1\text{A/s}$, the measured potential difference $V_{AB}$ between A and B is $6\text{V}$. The value of 'R' in the circuit is
66760.sol:
The potential difference between points A and B can be written using Kirchhoff's Voltage Law as:
$V_A - iR - L \dfrac{di}{dt} = V_B$
$\Rightarrow V_{AB} = V_A - V_B = iR + L \dfrac{di}{dt}$

Case 1: When the current is $3\text{ A}$ and increasing at $1\text{ A/s}$, we have $i = 3\text{ A}$ and $\dfrac{di}{dt} = 1\text{ A/s}$.
Given $V_{AB} = 12\text{ V}$, substituting the values:
$12 = 3R + L(1)$
$3R + L = 12$ ... (i)

Case 2: When the current is $3\text{ A}$ and decreasing at $1\text{ A/s}$, we have $i = 3\text{ A}$ and $\dfrac{di}{dt} = -1\text{ A/s}$.
Given $V_{AB} = 6\text{ V}$, substituting the values:
$6 = 3R + L(-1)$
$3R - L = 6$ ... (ii)

Adding equations (i) and (ii), we get:
$(3R + L) + (3R - L) = 12 + 6$
$6R = 18$
$R = 3\ \Omega$

Answer: $3\ \Omega$

67381.subject: Physics
67381.text: An ideal gas (\gamma = 1.5$) is expanded adiabatically. To reduce the root mean square velocity of molecules two times, the gas should be expanded$
67381.sol:
The root mean square velocity of gas molecules is given by $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$.

This implies $v_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$.

To reduce the rms velocity by a factor of $2$, the absolute temperature must be reduced by a factor of $4$. Thus, $T_f = \dfrac{T_i}{4}$.

For an adiabatic process, the relation between temperature and volume is $TV^{\gamma - 1} = \text{constant}$.

Therefore, $T_i V_i^{\gamma - 1} = T_f V_f^{\gamma - 1}$.

$\left( \dfrac{V_f}{V_i} \right)^{\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{T_i}{T_f}$

Given $\gamma = 1.5$, we have $\gamma - 1 = 0.5 = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

$\left( \dfrac{V_f}{V_i} \right)^{\dfrac{1}{2}} = 4$

$\dfrac{V_f}{V_i} = 4^2 = 16$

The gas should be expanded $16$ times.

Answer: $16$ times

67688.subject: Physics
67688.text: A square coil ABCD of side ' L ' is carrying a current in clockwise direction. A straight conductor carrying current $\mathrm{I}_2$ (upward direction) is kept parallel to side $A B$ at a distance $\frac{L}{3}$ in the plane of $A B C D$. The net force on the coil ABCD is ( $\mu_0=$ magnetic permeability)
67688.sol:
Magnetic force on a square coil near a straight current-carrying conductor

The straight conductor along the y-axis carrying current $I_2$ produces a magnetic field at perpendicular distance $x$ given by $B = \frac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi x}$, directed into the page ($-\hat{k}$) for $x > 0$ when $I_2$ flows upward.

For side AB, located at distance $L/3$ from the conductor with current $I_1$ flowing downward ($\vec{L}_{AB} = -L\hat{j}$), the magnetic field is $\vec{B}_{AB} = -\frac{3\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi L}\hat{k}$. The force is $\vec{F}_{AB} = I_1 (\vec{L}_{AB} \times \vec{B}_{AB}) = \frac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi}\hat{i}$.

For side CD, at distance $4L/3$ with current flowing upward ($\vec{L}_{CD} = L\hat{j}$), the magnetic field is $\vec{B}_{CD} = -\frac{3\mu_0 I_2}{8\pi L}\hat{k}$. The force is $\vec{F}_{CD} = I_1 (\vec{L}_{CD} \times \vec{B}_{CD}) = -\frac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}\hat{i}$.

The horizontal sides BC and DA experience forces that cancel exactly. For side BC, $d\vec{F}_{BC} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi x}\hat{j}dx$, yielding $\vec{F}_{BC} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi}\ln 4\hat{j}$ after integration from $x = L/3$ to $4L/3$. For side DA, the integration from $x = 4L/3$ to $L/3$ gives $\vec{F}_{DA} = -\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi}\ln 4\hat{j}$, so $\vec{F}_{BC} + \vec{F}_{DA} = 0$.

The net force on the coil is therefore $\vec{F}_{net} = \vec{F}_{AB} + \vec{F}_{CD} = \frac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi}\hat{i} - \frac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}\hat{i} = \frac{9\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}\hat{i}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\mathrm{D}}$

68040.text: The density of a cube is measured by measuring its mass and length of its sides. The % error in the measurement of mass and length are 5 % and $6 \%$ respectively. The percentage error in the measurement of density is
68040.sol:
The density of a cube is given by $\rho = M L^{-3}$, where $M$ is mass and $L$ is side length.

For quantities of the form $Q = A^x B^y$, the percentage error propagates as $\frac{\Delta Q}{Q} \times 100\% = |x| \frac{\Delta A}{A} \times 100\% + |y| \frac{\Delta B}{B} \times 100\%$.

Given $5\%$ error in mass measurement and $6\%$ error in length measurement:

$\frac{\Delta\rho}{\rho} \times 100\% = |1| \cdot 5\% + |-3| \cdot 6\% = 5\% + 18\% = 23\%$

The percentage error in density measurement is $\mathbf{23\%}$, corresponding to choice B.

68169.text: Water rises up to height ' $x$ ' in a capillary tube immersed vertically in water. When the whole arrangement is taken to a depth ' d ' in a mine, the water level rises up to height Y. If R is the radius of the earth then the ratio $\mathrm{Y}: \mathrm{x}$ is
68169.sol:
The capillary rise x at Earth's surface follows $x = \frac{2T \cos\theta}{\rho g r}$ with gravitational acceleration $g$.

At depth $d$, gravity becomes $g' = g(1 - \frac{d}{R})$, yielding a new rise height $Y = \frac{2T \cos\theta}{\rho g' r}$.

Substituting $g'$ gives $Y = \frac{2T \cos\theta}{\rho g r (1 - \frac{d}{R})}$.

The ratio simplifies as:

$\frac{Y}{x} = \frac{1}{1 - \frac{d}{R}} = \frac{R}{R-d}$

Thus $Y:x = R:(R-d)$, corresponding to option B.

68971.subject: Physics
68971.text: The phenomenon, which is not due to total internal reflection is
options: difference between apparent and real depth of a pond.
68971.sol:
Total internal reflection occurs when light attempts to pass from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle exceeding the critical angle, $i_c = \arcsin \left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right)$ for $ n_1 > n_2$.

Mirage formation involves refraction and TIR; light from the sky reflects off hot, rarer air layers near the ground.

Diamond brilliance results from multiple TIRs within the gem due to its high refractive index and low critical angle.

Apparent depth arises solely from refraction at the water-air interface, governed by $n_{\text{water}$} \sin \theta_{$\text{water}$} = n_{$\text{air}$} \sin \theta_{$\text{air}$}$, with no TIR involved.

Optical fibers rely on TIR; light reflects along the core-cladding interface when incidence exceeds $i_c$.

The phenomenon not due to total internal reflection is the difference between apparent and real depth of a pond.

The final answer is $\boxed{C}$.

$

71891.subject: Chemistry
71891.text: In the washing of precipitates, the wash liquid should contain a common ion with the precipitate for
options: increasing the ionisation and increasing the solubility
increasing the ionisation and decreasing the solubility
suppressing the ionisation and decreasing the solubility
suppressing the ionisation and increasing the solubility
71891.sol:
The addition of a common ion to the wash liquid suppresses the ionization (or dissociation) of the sparingly soluble precipitate due to the common ion effect.

According to Le Chatelier's principle, the presence of the common ion shifts the solubility equilibrium towards the undissociated solid precipitate.

This decreases the solubility of the precipitate, preventing its loss during the washing process.

Therefore, the wash liquid should contain a common ion for suppressing the ionization and decreasing the solubility.

Answer: suppressing the ionisation and decreasing the solubility

Let the oxidation number of sulfur in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ be $x$.

$2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0$

$2 + x - 8 = 0$

$x = +6$

Answer: $+6$

77316.text:
For the following two (02) items:
Consider the function $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{1 - x}$ (x > 0$, $x \neq 1$).

What is \dfrac{f(x)}{f(x+1)}$ equal to?
77316.sol:
Given $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{1 - x}$

Substitute $x+1$ for $x$ to find $f(x+1)$:

$f(x+1) = \dfrac{x+1}{1 - (x+1)} = \dfrac{x+1}{-x}$

Now, calculate the ratio $\dfrac{f(x)}{f(x+1)}$:

$\dfrac{f(x)}{f(x+1)} = \dfrac{\dfrac{x}{1 - x}}{\dfrac{x+1}{-x}}$

$\dfrac{f(x)}{f(x+1)} = \dfrac{x}{1 - x} \times \dfrac{-x}{x+1} = \dfrac{-x^2}{1 - x^2}$

Since $f(x^2) = \dfrac{x^2}{1 - x^2}$, we get:

77937.text:
Paragraph: Given that $C(n, r): C(n, r+1)=1: 2$ and $C(n, r+1): C(n, r+2)=2: 3$.
Question: What is $n$ equal to?
77937.sol:
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{{ }^n \mathrm{C}_r}{{ }^n \mathrm{C}_{r+1}}=\frac{1}{2} (given)\\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}}{\frac{n!}{(r+1)!(n-r-1)!}}=\frac{1}{2} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{(r+1)!(n-r-1)!}{r!(n-r)!}=\frac{1}{2} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{(r+1) \cdot r!(n-r-1)!}{r!(n-r)(n-r-1)!}=\frac{1}{2} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad n-r=2(r+1) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad n-r=2 r+2 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad n=3 r+2 ..(i)\\
& \text{ Again, } \\
& \frac{{ }^n C_{r+1}}{{ }^n C_{r+2}}=\frac{2}{3}
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\frac{n!}{(r+1)!(n-r-1)!}}{\frac{n!}{(r+2)!(n-r-2)!}}=\frac{2}{3} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{(r+2)!(n-r-2)!}{(r+1)!(n-r-1)!}=\frac{2}{3} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{(r+2)(r+1)!(n-r-2)!}{(r+1)!(n-r-1)(n-r-2)!}=\frac{2}{3} \\
& 2(n-r-1)=3(r+2) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 2 n-2 r-2=3 r+6 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 2 n=5 r+8...(ii)
\end{aligned}$
Multiply equation (i) by 2
$2 n=6 r+4$ ...(iii)
From equations (ii) and (iii)
$\begin{aligned}
& & 6 r+4 & =5 r+8 \\
\Rightarrow & & r & =4
\end{aligned}$
Putting the value of $r$ in equation (ii)
$\begin{aligned}
2 n & =5(4)+8 \\
2 n & =20+8 \\
2 n & =28 \\
n & =14 .
\end{aligned}$
Value of $n=14$.

78343.subject: Mathematics
78343.text: If $p$ times the $p^{\text{th }}$ term of an AP is equal to $q$ times the $q^{\text{th }}$ term $(p \neq q)$, then what is the $(p+q)^{\text{th }}$ term equal to?
78343.sol:
Suppose 'a' and 'd' be the first term and common difference of AP respectively.
$\begin{aligned}
& \because \mathrm{n}^{\text{th }} \text{ term }=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{n}}=\mathrm{a}+(\mathrm{n}-1) \cdot \mathrm{d}\\
& \therefore \quad(\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{q})^{\text{th }} \text{ term }=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{q}}=\mathrm{a}+(\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{q}-1) \mathrm{d}....(i)
\end{aligned}$
Given, $\mathrm{p} \cdot \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{q} \cdot \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{q}}\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{p} \cdot[\mathrm{a}+(\mathrm{p}-1) \mathrm{d}]=\mathrm{q} \cdot[\mathrm{a}+(\mathrm{q}-1) \mathrm{d}] \\
& \Rightarrow(\mathrm{p}-\mathrm{q})[\mathrm{a}+(\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{q}-1) \mathrm{d}]=0 \\
& \Rightarrow[\mathrm{a}+(\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{q}-1) \mathrm{d}]=0 \quad\{\because \mathrm{p} \neq \mathrm{q}\} \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{q}}=0 \quad\{\text{$ from $}(\mathrm{i})\}
\end{aligned}$

79842.subject: Botany
79842.text: During meiosis $I,$ in which stage synapsis takes place?
79842.sol:
Prophase I is subdivided into five phases, viz. Leptotene, Zygotene, Pachytene, Diplotene and Diakinesis.

Leptotene: During this stage, the chromosomes become gradually visible under a light microscope. Compaction of chromosomes continues throughout this phase.

Zygotene: Chromosomes start pairing together. This process is called synapsis. The paired chromosomes are called homologous chromosomes. The formation of synapsis is accompanied by the formation of the synaptonemal complex.

Pachytene: Recombination nodules appear. These nodules are the sites at which crossing over takes place between non-sister chromatids of the homologous chromosomes.

Diplotene: Synapotnemal complex is dissolved at this stage. The recombined homologous chromosomes of the bivalent separate from each other; except at the site of crossing over. The X-shaped structures; thus formed; are called chiasmata.

Diakinesis: Chiasmata is terminated at this stage.

81268.subject: Chemistry
81268.text:
The lanthanide ion having four unpaired electrons is
(Given : Atomic numbers of Ce $=58$, Nd $=60$, Tb $=65$ and Ho $=67$)
81268.sol:
The general electronic configuration of lanthanide ions $\text{Ln}^{3+}$ is $[\text{Xe}] 4f^{Z-57}$, where $Z$ is the atomic number.

For $\text{Ho}^{3+}$ ($Z=67$):
Number of $4f$ electrons $= 67 - 57 = 10$
Configuration is $[\text{Xe}] 4f^{10}$.
Since the $f$-subshell has 7 orbitals, 10 electrons will fill as 3 pairs and 4 unpaired electrons. Number of unpaired electrons $= 14 - 10 = 4$.

For $\text{Nd}^{3+}$ ($Z=60$):
Number of $4f$ electrons $= 60 - 57 = 3$
Configuration is $[\text{Xe}] 4f^{3}$.
Number of unpaired electrons $= 3$.

For $\text{Ce}^{3+}$ ($Z=58$):
Number of $4f$ electrons $= 58 - 57 = 1$
Configuration is $[\text{Xe}] 4f^{1}$.
Number of unpaired electrons $= 1$.

For $\text{Tb}^{3+}$ ($Z=65$):
Number of $4f$ electrons $= 65 - 57 = 8$
Configuration is $[\text{Xe}] 4f^{8}$.
Number of unpaired electrons $= 14 - 8 = 6$.

Thus, $\text{Ho}^{3+}$ has exactly four unpaired electrons.

Answer: $\text{Ho}^{3+}$

81870.sol:
Given, molarity $=2 \mathrm{M}$ [i.e 2 mole $\mathrm{NaOH}$ in $1 \mathrm{~L}$ solution]
Density $(\mathrm{d})=1.28 \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}$
Molecular weight of $\mathrm{NaOH}=40 \mathrm{gmol}^{-1}$
We know that,

$\begin{aligned}$& $\text{ Density }=\frac{\text{ mass$ of $solution }}{\text{ volume of solution }}$\\
& \therefore $\text{ Mass$ of solution }=1.28 $\mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \times$1000 $\mathrm{~mL}=$1280 $\mathrm{~g}$\\
& $\text{ Moreover, molarity }$\\
& =$\frac{\text{ number$ of $moles of solute }}{\text{ volume of solution }(\text{ in } \mathrm{mL})} \times$1000 \\
& \therefore \quad 2=$\frac{\text{ mass$ of $solute }}{40 \times 1000} \times$1000=80 $\mathrm{~g}$\\
& $\text{ Now, mass$ of $solution }=\text{ mass of solvent }+ \text{ mass of }$\\
& $\text{ solute }$\\
& 1280 $\mathrm{~g}=\text{ mass$ of solvent }+80 \\
& \therefore$\text{ Mass$ of solvent }=1280-80=1200 $\mathrm{~g}=$1.2 $\mathrm{~kg}$\\
& $\text{ Now, molality }=\frac{\text{ number$ of $moles of solute }}{\text{ mass of solvent }(\text{ in kg) }}$\\
& =$\frac{2}{1.2}=\frac{20}{12}=\frac{5}{3}=$1.67 $\mathrm{~m}$\\
&
\end{aligned}

Alternative method
Molality $(\mathrm{m})=\frac{\mathrm{M}}{1000 \mathrm{~d}-\mathrm{M} \omega \mathrm{t}} \times 1000$
where, $M=$ molarity, $d=$ density of solution

$\mathrm{M} \omega \mathrm{t}=\text{ molar mass of solute. }On substing the given values, we get

$\begin{aligned}$\text{ Molality }$& =$\frac{2}{1000 \times 1.28-40} \times$1000 \\
& =$\frac{2}{1280-40} \times$1000=$\frac{2000}{1240}=$1.612 $\mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}$

Given, $\mathrm{B}=3 \times 10^{-8} \cos \left(1.6 \times 10^3 x\right.$ $\left.+48 \times 10^{10} t\right)$
On comparing equations (1) & (2), we get;
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{B}_0 & =3 \times 10^{-8} \\
c & =\frac{\omega}{k}=\frac{48 \times 10^{10}}{1.6 \times 10^3} \\
& =3 \times 10^8
\end{aligned}$
And also, $c=\frac{\mathrm{E}_0}{\mathrm{~B}_0}$
Hence, $E_0=B_0 \times c$
$\begin{aligned}
& =3 \times 10^{-8} \times 3 \times 10^8 \\
& =9
\end{aligned}$
So, the required equation is:
$\mathrm{E}=9 \cos \left(1.6 \times 10^3 x+48 \times 10^{10} t\right)$

85993.subject: Chemistry
85993.text:
Consider the following compound.

The compound reacts with $\text{SOCl}_2$ to produce P. P reacts with dimethyl cadmium to produce Q. Q upon reaction with ethyl magnesium bromide (3 equiv) followed by water workup produces R. The structure of R is:
85993.sol:
The starting compound is $CH_3O-CO-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-COOH$, which contains both a methyl ester and a carboxylic acid group.

Reaction with $SOCl_2$ selectively converts the carboxylic acid group ($-COOH$) into an acid chloride group ($-COCl$). The ester group remains unaffected.

Compound P is $CH_3O-CO-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-COCl$.

Dimethyl cadmium ($(CH_3)_2Cd$) is a mild organometallic reagent that specifically reacts with acid chlorides to form ketones, but it does not react with esters. It replaces the $-Cl$ with a $-CH_3$ group.

Compound Q is $CH_3O-CO-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-COCH_3$.

Compound Q possesses a methyl ester group and a methyl ketone group. It is treated with $3$ equivalents of ethyl magnesium bromide ($CH_3CH_2MgBr$), a Grignard reagent.

The methyl ketone group reacts with $1$ equivalent of the Grignard reagent, adding one ethyl group to form a tertiary alkoxide: $-COCH_3 \rightarrow -C(O^{-})(CH_3)(CH_2CH_3)$.

The methyl ester group reacts with $2$ equivalents of the Grignard reagent. The first equivalent displaces the methoxide leaving group to form an ethyl ketone intermediate, which rapidly reacts with the second equivalent to form a tertiary alkoxide with two ethyl groups: $-COOCH_3 \rightarrow -C(O^{-})(CH_2CH_3)_2$.

A total of $3$ equivalents are consumed. Subsequent water workup protonates these alkoxides to form the corresponding alcohols.

The final product R is $HO-C(CH_2CH_3)_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-C(OH)(CH_3)(CH_2CH_3)$.

Comparing this with the given options, the structure corresponds to option (3), which has two ethyl groups on the left carbon and one ethyl and one methyl group on the right carbon.

Answer :

90987.text: Let $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{9x}{25} + c, c > 0 .$ If the curve $y = {f}^{- 1}\left(x\right)$ passes through $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}, - \dfrac{5}{4}\right)$ and g$\left(x\right) is the antiderivative of ${f}^{- 1}$\left(x\right)$ such that $g\left(0\right) = \dfrac{5}{2},$ then the value of $\left[g\left(1\right)\right]$ is, (where $[ . ]$ represents the greatest integer function)
90987.sol:
$y = f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{9x}{25} + {c}_{1}$
$⇒ x = \dfrac{25}{9}\left(y - {c}_{1}\right) = {f}^{- 1}\left(y\right)$
$⇒ {f}^{- 1}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{25}{9}\left(x - {c}_{1}\right)$
The curve $y = {f}^{- 1}\left(x\right)$ passes through $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}, - \dfrac{5}{9}\right)$
$⇒ - \dfrac{5}{9} = \dfrac{25}{9}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - {c}_{1}\right)$
$⇒ {c}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{5} = \dfrac{9}{20}$
$⇒ {f}^{- 1}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{25}{9}\left(x - \dfrac{9}{20}\right)$ $= \dfrac{25x}{9} - \dfrac{5}{4}$
$g\left(x\right) = ∫ {f}^{- 1}\left(x\right)dx = ‍ ∫ \left(\dfrac{25x}{9} - \dfrac{5}{4}\right)dx‍$
$= \dfrac{25}{9}\left(\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right) - \dfrac{5x}{4} + {c}_{2}$

91678.text: If $4$ letter words are formed using letters of the word ‘MORADABAD’, then the probability that D comes exactly once in the $4$ letter word is
91678.sol:
Total cases $= 4$ letter word is formed by using either $3$ identical letter and $1$ distinct letter or $2$ alike of one kind and $2$ alike of ${2}^{nd}$ kind or $2$ alike, $2$ distinct or $4$ distinct
Number of ways for $3$ alike and $1$ distinct $= {C 1}_{1} \times {C 5}_{1} \times \dfrac{4 !}{3 !} = 20$
Number of ways for $2$ alike and $2$ alike $= {C 2}_{2} \times \dfrac{4 !}{2 ! 2 !} = 6$
Number of ways for $2$ alike and $2$ distinct $= {C 2}_{1} \times {C 5}_{2} \times \dfrac{4 !}{2 !} = 240$
Number of ways for $4$ distinct $= {C 6}_{4} \times 4 ! = 360$
The total number of ways $= 20 + 6 + 240 + 360 = 626$
For favorable cases, the following possibilities are there (one D is always included)
Number of ways for $3$ alike $= C1 1 \times \dfrac{4 !}{3 !} = 4$
Number of ways for $2$ alike $+ 1$ distinct $= C1 1 \times C1 4 \times \dfrac{4 !}{2 !} = 48$
Number of ways for $3$ distinct $= C3 5 \times 4 ! = 240$
The total number of ways for favorable cases $= 240 + 48 + 4 = 292$
Hence, the required probability $= \dfrac{292}{626} = \dfrac{146}{313}$

$\alpha + 4\beta = 6, \alpha\left(4\beta\right) = a$
$\alpha + 3\beta = c, \alpha\left(3\beta\right) = 6 ⇒ \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{a}{6} ⇒ \alpha = 8$
The first equation is $x^{2} - 6x + 8 = 0$
Whose roots are $2$ and $4$
If $\alpha = 2 ⇒ \beta = 1$
So, roots of first equation is $2, 4$ and that of second equation is $2, 3$
If $\alpha = 4 ⇒ \beta = \dfrac{1}{2} ⇒ 3\beta = \dfrac{3}{2}, 4\beta = 2$
Here the roots are not integers $⇒ \alpha = 2$

Therefore the sum of $ n$ terms is
${S}_{n} = {u}_{1} + {u}_{2} + . . . . + {u}_{n}$
$= $\dfrac{1}{4}\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{n}$ k^{2} + $\dfrac{n}{16} + \dfrac{1}{32} \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2n + 1}\right)
$= $\dfrac{n\left(n + 1\right)\left(2n + 1\right)}{4.6} + \dfrac{n}{16} + \dfrac{n}{16\left(2n + 1\right)}
$= $\dfrac{n\left(n + 1\right)\left(n^{2} + n + 1\right)}{6\left(2n + 1\right)}$

92600.text: Two particles of equal mass have velocities $\overset{→}{v}1 = 4\overset{^}{i}\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$ and $\overset{→}{v}2 = 4\overset{^}{j}{  ms}^{- 1}$. The centre of mass of the two particles moves in a path of
92600.sol:
Since, ${m}_{1} = {m}_{2} = m$

$\overset{→}{v} \text{cm} = \dfrac{{m}_{1} \overset{→}{v} 1 + {m}_{2} \overset{→}{v} 2}{{m}_{1} + {m}_{2}} = \dfrac{m}{2m} \left(\overset{→}{v}1 + \overset{→}{v} 2\right)$
$= \dfrac{1}{2} \times (4\overset{^}{i} + 4\overset{^}{j} )$

$= 2 ( \overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} )$

Similarly $\overset{→}{a} \text{cm} = \dfrac{{m}_{1} \overset{→}{{a}_{1}} + {m}_{2} \overset{→}{{a}_{2}}}{{m}_{1} + {m}_{2}} = \dfrac{m}{2m} ( \overset{→}{{a}_{1}} + \overset{→}{{a}_{2}} )$

$= \dfrac{5}{2} ( \overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} )$

Both $\overset{→}{v} cm$ and $\overset{→}{a} cm$ are parallel

Centre of mass will move in a straight line because velocity and acceleration of centre of mass are in same direction.

$\left|\dfrac{dN}{dt}\right|$= |Activity of radioactive substance|

$= \lambdaN = \lambda{N}_{0}e^{- \lambdat} ( ∵ N = {N}_{0}e^{- \lambdat} )$

Taking log both sides

Hence, ln$\left|\dfrac{dN}{dt}\right|$~versus& $t$ graph is a straight line with slope-$\lambda$.

From the graph, we can see that,

$\lambda = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5{yr}^{- 1}$

Now applying the equation

$N = {N}_{0}e^{- \lambdat} = {N}_{0}e^{- 0.5 \times 4.16}$

$= {N}_{0}e^{- 2.08} = {N}_{0}e^{- 2 \times \left(0 . 693\right)} = 0.125{N}_{0}$

$= \dfrac{{N}_{0}}{8}$

i.e. nuclei decrease by a factor of $8$.

Hence the answer is $8$.

100677.subject: Physics
100677.text: A train starts from rest and moves on a straight horizontal track with uniform acceleration. It covers a distance of $40$ m in $4$ s. A box resting on the floor of the train is observed to be just on the verge of slipping. What is the coefficient of static friction between the box and the floor of the train? (Take $g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$)
100677.sol:
Let the acceleration of the train be $a$.

Using the second equation of motion:
$S = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$
$40 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times a \times (4)^2$
$40 = 8a \Rightarrow a = 5$ m s$^{-2}$

For the box to be just on the verge of slipping, the pseudo force on it in the frame of the train must be equal to the limiting static friction.
$ma = \mu_s mg$
$\mu_s = \dfrac{a}{g}$

Substituting the values:
$\mu_s = \dfrac{5}{10} = 0.5$

Answer: $0.5$

100705.subject: Physics
100705.text: A uniform rod is placed leaning against a smooth vertical wall and resting on a rough horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction between the rod and the floor is $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$. What is the minimum angle the rod can make with the horizontal floor without slipping?
100705.sol:
Let the mass of the rod be $m$, its length be $L$, and the angle it makes with the horizontal floor be $\theta$.

The forces acting on the rod are:
1. Weight $mg$ acting vertically downwards from the center of mass ($L/2$ from either end).
2. Normal reaction from the floor $N_f$ acting vertically upwards.
3. Normal reaction from the wall $N_w$ acting horizontally outwards.
4. Static friction $f$ acting horizontally inwards at the floor.

For translational equilibrium:
$\Sigma F_y = 0 \Rightarrow N_f = mg$
$\Sigma F_x = 0 \Rightarrow f = N_w$

For rotational equilibrium, taking torque about the point of contact with the floor:
$N_w \times L \sin\theta - mg \times \dfrac{L}{2} \cos\theta = 0$
$N_w = \dfrac{mg}{2 \tan\theta}$

Since $f = N_w$, the required friction force is $f = \dfrac{mg}{2 \tan\theta}$.

To prevent slipping, the friction force must not exceed the limiting static friction:
$f \le \mu N_f$
$\dfrac{mg}{2 \tan\theta} \le \mu mg$
$\dfrac{1}{2 \tan\theta} \le \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$
$\tan\theta \ge \sqrt{3}$

The minimum angle $\theta$ is therefore $60^{\circ}$.

Answer: $60^{\circ}$

100996.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
100996.text:
Statement-I: When you lean behind over the hind legs of the chair, the chair falls back after a certain angle.
Statement-II: Centre of mass lying outside the system makes the system unstable.

Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.
Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect.
Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.
100996.sol:
- Stability criterion: an object is stable as long as the vertical line through its centre of mass (CM) falls inside the base of support. If the vertical from the CM passes outside the base, the normal reaction can no longer provide a balancing moment and the object will tip.
- Apply to the chair. when you lean back on the hind legs you tilt the chair so the projection of the combined CM (you + chair) moves toward the back edge of the base. At a certain tilt angle the vertical through the CM crosses the rear edge - beyond that the CM lies outside the support polygon and the chair rotates (falls) backward. That is exactly Statement-I and it follows from Statement-II.
So both statements are true and related: the chair falls when the CM's vertical leaves the base of support.

101031.subject: Physics
101031.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
101031.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A moving body always rebounds in the opposite direction after a head-on elastic collision with a stationary target of a different mass.
Reason (R): In a one-dimensional elastic collision, a moving body of mass $m$ transfers the exact same fraction of its initial kinetic energy to a stationary target of mass $2m$ as it does to a stationary target of mass $m/2$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
101031.sol:
Evaluate Assertion (A):
The final velocity of a moving body of mass $m_1$ colliding elastically with a stationary target of mass $m_2$ is $v_1 = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}u_1$.
The body only rebounds (i.e., $v_1$ is negative) if $m_1 < m_2$. If $m_1 > m_2$, it continues moving in the same direction. Therefore, it does not always rebound when the masses are different. Assertion (A) is false.

Evaluate Reason (R):
The fraction of kinetic energy transferred to a stationary target is $f = \dfrac{4m_1 m_2}{(m_1 + m_2)^2}$.
For a target of mass $2m$: $f = \dfrac{4(m)(2m)}{(m + 2m)^2} = \dfrac{8m^2}{9m^2} = \dfrac{8}{9}$.
For a target of mass $m/2$: $f = \dfrac{4(m)(m/2)}{(m + m/2)^2} = \dfrac{2m^2}{(1.5m)^2} = \dfrac{2}{2.25} = \dfrac{8}{9}$.
The fraction transferred is identical in both cases. Reason (R) is true.

Thus, (A) is false but (R) is true.

Answer: (A) is false but (R) is true

101037.subject: Physics
101037.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
101037.text: A stationary nucleus of mass number $A$ undergoes alpha decay by emitting an alpha particle of mass $4$. If the total kinetic energy released in the reaction is $Q$, what is the kinetic energy of the recoiling daughter nucleus?
101037.sol:
Let the momentum of the emitted alpha particle be $p$. By the law of conservation of linear momentum, the recoiling daughter nucleus must have an equal and opposite momentum of magnitude $p$.

The mass of the alpha particle is $4$ and the mass of the daughter nucleus is $(A-4)$.

The kinetic energy of the alpha particle is $K_{\alpha} = \dfrac{p^2}{2(4)}$ and the kinetic energy of the daughter nucleus is $K_D = \dfrac{p^2}{2(A-4)}$.

The total kinetic energy released is $Q = K_{\alpha} + K_D = \dfrac{p^2}{2(4)} + \dfrac{p^2}{2(A-4)}$.

Simplifying the expression for $Q$:
$Q = \dfrac{p^2}{2} \left( \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{A-4} \right) = \dfrac{p^2}{2} \left( \dfrac{A-4+4}{4(A-4)} \right) = \dfrac{p^2}{2} \left( \dfrac{A}{4(A-4)} \right)$.

We need to find $K_D$ in terms of $Q$. Taking the ratio:
$\dfrac{K_D}{Q} = \dfrac{\dfrac{p^2}{2(A-4)}}{\dfrac{p^2}{2} \left( \dfrac{A}{4(A-4)} \right)} = \dfrac{4}{A}$.

Thus, the kinetic energy of the recoiling daughter nucleus is $K_D = \dfrac{4Q}{A}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{4Q}{A}$

102007.text:
Statement - I : When $\mu$ amount of an ideal gas undergoes adiabatic change from state $\left({P}_{1}, {V}_{1}, {T}_{1}\right)$ to state $\left({P}_{2}, {V}_{2}, {T}_{2}\right)$, then work done is $W = \dfrac{\muR\left({T}_{2} - {T}_{1}\right)}{1 - \gamma}$, where $\gamma = \dfrac{{C}_{P}}{{C}_{V}}$ and R = universal gas constant.

Statement - II : In the above case, when work is done on the gas, the temperature of the gas would rise.
options: Both statement-I and statement-II are true.
Both statement-I and statement-II are false.
Statement-I is true but statement-II is false.
Statement-I is false but statement-II is true.
102007.sol:
The work done in an adiabatic process is given by,

${W}_{adiabatic} = \dfrac{nR\left({T}_{f} - {T}_{i}\right)}{1 - \gamma} \to$ statement I is true.

For adiabatic process $∆ Q = 0$. From the first law of thermodynamics,

$∆ Q = W + \DeltaU$

$0 = W + \DeltaU$

$\DeltaU = - W$

If work is done on the gas, i.e. work is negative

$∴ \DeltaU$ is positive.

$∴$ The temperature will increase. Hence, statement II is also true.

102871.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For an electric dipole of finite length $2a$, the electric potential at a distance $r$ (where $r > a$) on the axial line near the positive charge is strictly greater than $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^2}$.

Reason (R): The exact electric potential at this point is proportional to $\dfrac{1}{r^2 - a^2}$, and since $(r^2 - a^2) < r^2$, the exact potential exceeds the approximate value.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
102871.sol:
The exact electric potential at a distance $r$ on the axial line of a dipole (closer to the positive charge) is given by:
$V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^2 - a^2}$

The approximate electric potential for a short dipole is:
$V_{\text{approx}} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^2}$

Since the point is at a distance $r > a$, the denominator of the exact formula $(r^2 - a^2)$ is strictly less than $r^2$.

Because the denominator is smaller, the overall fraction is larger. Therefore, $V > V_{\text{approx}}$.

Thus, Assertion (A) is correct. Reason (R) correctly states the mathematical relationship and provides the correct explanation for the Assertion.

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : When an extemal resistor of resistance R (connected across a cell of internal resistance r) is varied, power consumed by resistance \(R\) is maximum when \(R=r\).

103217.sol:
- Assertion (A): The power consumed by an external resistor \(R\) connected to a cell of internal resistance \(r\) is maximum when \(R=\). This is known as the condition for maximum power transfer, where the external resistance is equal to the internal resistance of the power source. So, Assertion (A) is true.
- Reason (R): Power consumed by a resistor is not necessarily maximum when the current through it is maximum. In fact, if the current is maximum, that typically means \(R\) is very small, leading to lower power consumption (since \(P=I^2 R\)). The maximum power occurs when \(R=r\), not when the current is at its maximum. Hence, Reason (R) is false.

103666.subject: Physics
103666.text:
A uniform electric field and a uniform magnetic field are acting along the same direction in a certain region. Match the particles and their initial projection directions in List-I with their resulting trajectories and kinetic energy changes in List-II.

List-IList-II
(A) Proton projected parallel to the fields(P) Straight line, kinetic energy increases
(B) Electron projected parallel to the fields(Q) Straight line, kinetic energy decreases
(C) Proton projected perpendicular to the fields(R) Helical path with increasing pitch
(D) Neutron projected perpendicular to the fields(S) Straight line, constant kinetic energy
103666.sol:
Let the electric field $\vec{E}$ and magnetic field $\vec{B}$ be along the x-axis.

(A) Proton projected parallel to the fields: Velocity $\vec{v}$ is parallel to $\vec{B}$, so magnetic force $F_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) = 0$. The electric force $\vec{F}_e = e\vec{E}$ acts in the direction of motion, causing the proton to accelerate in a straight line. Thus, its kinetic energy increases. (A) matches (P).

(B) Electron projected parallel to the fields: Velocity $\vec{v}$ is parallel to $\vec{B}$, so $F_m = 0$. The electric force $\vec{F}_e = -e\vec{E}$ acts opposite to the direction of motion, causing the electron to decelerate in a straight line. Thus, its kinetic energy decreases. (B) matches (Q).

(C) Proton projected perpendicular to the fields: Velocity $\vec{v}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{B}$, so the magnetic force provides a centripetal force, causing circular motion. Simultaneously, the electric force $\vec{F}_e = e\vec{E}$ accelerates the proton along the fields. The combined motion is a helical path with increasing pitch. (C) matches (R).

(D) Neutron projected perpendicular to the fields: A neutron is uncharged ($q = 0$), so it experiences zero electric and magnetic forces. It will continue to move in a straight line with constant velocity and constant kinetic energy. (D) matches (S).

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(P), (B)-(Q), (C)-(R), (D)-(S).

Answer: (A)-(P), (B)-(Q), (C)-(R), (D)-(S)

104134.subject: Physics
104134.text: A series $L-C-R$ circuit is connected to a variable frequency ac source of voltage amplitude $20\text{ V}$. The maximum current amplitude in the circuit is $2\text{ A}$. The angular frequencies at which the current amplitude drops to $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ of its maximum value are $95\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ and $105\text{ rad s}^{-1}$. The Quality factor ($Q$) of the circuit and the voltage amplitude across the inductor at resonance are respectively:
104134.sol:
The resonant angular frequency $\omega_0$ is the average of the half-power frequencies:

$\omega_0 = \dfrac{95 + 105}{2} = 100\text{ rad s}^{-1}$

The bandwidth $\Delta \omega$ is the difference between the half-power frequencies:

$\Delta \omega = 105 - 95 = 10\text{ rad s}^{-1}$

The Quality factor $Q$ is given by:

$Q = \dfrac{\omega_0}{\Delta \omega} = \dfrac{100}{10} = 10$

At resonance, the voltage amplitude across the inductor $V_L$ is $Q$ times the source voltage amplitude:

$V_L = Q \times V_{\text{source}} = 10 \times 20\text{ V} = 200\text{ V}$

Answer: $10$ and $200\text{ V}$

108689.text:
Consider the thermochemical equation for the synthesis of ammonia:
$\mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 3\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{g}) \quad \Delta_{\mathrm{r}}\mathrm{H}^{\circ} = -92.4 \mathrm{~kJ}$

What is the standard enthalpy change for the decomposition of one mole of ammonia gas into its constituent elements?
108689.sol:
The given reaction is the formation of $2$ moles of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ with $\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}\mathrm{H}^{\circ} = -92.4 \mathrm{~kJ}$.

The decomposition of ammonia is the reverse reaction:
$2\mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 3\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g})$
For this reverse reaction, the sign of the enthalpy change is reversed:
$\Delta\mathrm{H}^{\circ} = +92.4 \mathrm{~kJ}$ for the decomposition of $2$ moles of $\mathrm{NH}_3$.

For the decomposition of $1$ mole of $\mathrm{NH}_3$, the enthalpy change is:
$\Delta\mathrm{H}^{\circ} = \dfrac{+92.4}{2} = +46.2 \mathrm{~kJ}$.

Answer: $+46.2 \mathrm{~kJ}$

108955.subject: Chemistry
108955.text:
Consider the exothermic oxidation of sulfur dioxide at equilibrium:

$2\mathrm{SO}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{SO}_3(\mathrm{g}) + \text{Heat}$

Which of the following actions will decrease the equilibrium yield of $\mathrm{SO}_3$?
options: Adding an inert gas at constant volume
Adding an inert gas at constant pressure
108955.sol:
The given reaction is exothermic. According to Le Chatelier's principle, decreasing the temperature will shift the equilibrium in the forward direction, increasing the yield of $\mathrm{SO}_3$.

The number of gaseous moles on the reactant side is $2 + 1 = 3$, and on the product side is $2$. Since $\Delta n_g = 2 - 3 = -1$, increasing the pressure will shift the equilibrium towards the side with fewer gaseous moles (forward direction), increasing the yield of $\mathrm{SO}_3$.

Adding an inert gas at constant volume does not change the partial pressures or molar concentrations of the reacting gases, so the equilibrium state is unaffected.

Adding an inert gas at constant pressure increases the total volume of the system. This decreases the partial pressures of all reacting gases, causing the equilibrium to shift towards the direction with more gaseous moles (backward direction) to oppose the change. This backward shift will decrease the equilibrium yield of $\mathrm{SO}_3$.

Answer: Adding an inert gas at constant pressure

111827.text: Give a brief description of Chromatography taking an example.
options: Chromatography is a process in which a mixture is separated into its components based on their chemical reactivity. The mixture is passed through a column filled with an adsorbent, and the components are separated based on their affinity for the adsorbent. An example is the separation of amino acids using thin-layer chromatography.

Chromatography is a process in which a mixture is separated into its components based on their solubility in a solvent. The mixture is dissolved in a solvent, and the soluble components are separated from the insoluble ones. An example is the extraction of caffeine from coffee beans.

Chromatography is a process in which a mixture is separated into its components based on their size and shape. The mixture is passed through a gel filtration column, and the components are separated based on their ability to penetrate the gel. An example is the separation of proteins by size exclusion chromatography.

Chromatography is a process in which a mixture is separated into its components based on their affinity for a stationary phase and a mobile phase. The mixture is introduced onto a stationary phase, and the components are separated as they move through the stationary phase with the mobile phase. An example is the separation of pigments in ink using paper chromatography.
111827.sol:
Correct Option is : (D)
Chromatography is a process in which a mixture is separated into its components based on their affinity for a stationary phase and a mobile phase. This independence from initial concentration is a characteristic feature of a first-order reaction.

Answer: $1$

116193.subject: Chemistry
116193.text:
Observe the following statements :
a. The thermal stability of hydrides of group 16 elements follow the order :
$\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}>\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}>\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Se}>\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Te}$
b. Acidic nature of hydrides of group 16 elements follow the order :
$\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}>\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}>\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Se}>\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Te}$
c. The reducing nature of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}, \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Se}$ and $\mathrm{H}_2$ Te follow the order :
$\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S} < \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Se} < \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Te}$
The correct statement are:
116193.sol:
- a. The thermal stability of hydrides of group 16 elements follows the order: \($\mathrm{H}}_{2}  \mathrm{O}  \gt  \mathrm{H}$}_{2} $\mathrm{~S}  \gt  \mathrm{H}}_{2}  \mathrm{Se}  \gt  \mathrm{H}$}_{2} $\mathrm{Te}$\) This is correct. As you go down the group, the central atom's size increases, and the E-H bond length increases. The bond becomes weaker and easier to break with heat, so thermal stability decreases.
- b. The acidic nature of hydrides of group 16 elements follows the order: \($\mathrm{H}}_{2}  \mathrm{O}  \gt  \mathrm{H}$}_{2} $\mathrm{~S}  \gt  \mathrm{H}}_{2}  \mathrm{Se}  \gt  \mathrm{H}$}_{2} $\mathrm{Te}$\) This is incorrect. The acidic nature increases down the group. As the E-H bond becomes weaker, it is easier to break, making it easier to donate a proton ( \(H^{+}\)). The correct order is \($\mathrm{H}}_{2}  \mathrm{O} \lt  \mathrm{H}$}_{2} $\mathrm{~S} \lt  \mathrm{H}}_{2}  \mathrm{Se} \lt  \mathrm{H}$}_{2} $\mathrm{Te}$\).
- c. The reducing nature of \($\mathrm{H}}_{2}  \mathrm{~S}, \mathrm{H}$}_{2} $\mathrm{Se}$\), and \($\mathrm{H}}_{2} $\mathrm{Te}$\) follows the order: \( \mathrm{H}$}_{2} $\mathrm{~S} \lt  \mathrm{H}}_{2}  \mathrm{Se} \lt  \mathrm{H}$}_{2} $\mathrm{Te}$\) This is correct. The reducing nature increases as the E-H bond strength decreases down the group. It is easier for the hydride to donate hydrogen and get oxidized as the bond gets weaker.

120977.subject: Chemistry
120977.text: Which of the following amino acids contains nitrogen in its side chain but is classified as a neutral amino acid?
120977.sol:
Amino acids are classified as acidic, basic, or neutral depending upon the relative number of amino and carboxyl groups in their molecule. Equal number of amino and carboxyl groups makes it neutral; more number of amino than carboxyl groups makes it basic.

Histidine, Arginine, and Lysine contain basic nitrogenous groups in their side chains, making them basic amino acids. Glutamine contains an amide group ($-\text{CONH}_2$) in its side chain. The nitrogen lone pair in an amide is involved in resonance with the carbonyl group, rendering it non-basic. Since Glutamine has one $\alpha$-amino group and one $\alpha$-carboxyl group, it is classified as a neutral amino acid.

Answer: Glutamine

121622.text: "Ordines Anomali" of Bentham and Hooker includes
options: seed plants showing abnormal forms of growth and development
plants described only in fossil state
plants described in the literature but which Bentham and Hooker did not see in original
a few orders which could not be placed satisfactorily in the classification.
121622.sol: The system of classification of seed plants presented by Bentham and Hooker, represented the most well developed classification of natural system. The classification was published in 3 volumes of 'Genera plantarum'. The system divided phanerogams or seed plants into 3 classes dicotyledons, gymnospermae and monocotyledons. Dicotyledons were further subdivided into 3 subclasses - polypetalae, gamopetalae and monochlamydae based on the presence or absence of petals and their fusion. They were further divided into series, orders and families. No orders were recognised within monochlamydae and monocotyledons, the series being directly divided into families. But the system had a lot of demerits within it. He did not know the affinities of the families placed under 'Ordines anomate' and the families were tentativily grouped together. So, a few orders were not placed satisfactorily in the classification. Monochlamydae is an unnatural assemblage of taxa, which belongs elsewhere. The creation of this group has resulted in the separation of many closely related families.

124414.sol: The common feature between eukaryotic and prokaryotic flagella is that both are used for locomotion. Prokaryotic flagellum is single stranded while eukaryotic flagellum is 11-stranded. Prokaryotic and eukaryotic flagellum are made up of flagellin and tubulin proteins, respectively.

125652.subject: Botany
125652.text: What is the total number of ATP and NADPH molecules required to synthesize one molecule of glucose during the biosynthetic phase in a maize plant?
125652.sol:
Maize is a $C_{4}$ plant. In the $C_{4}$ pathway, the fixation of one $CO_{2}$ molecule requires 5 ATP (3 ATP for the Calvin cycle in the bundle sheath cells and 2 ATP for the regeneration of PEP in the mesophyll cells) and 2 NADPH.

To synthesize one molecule of glucose, 6 molecules of $CO_{2}$ must be fixed.

Therefore, the total energy requirement is $6 \times 5 = 30$ ATP and $6 \times 2 = 12$ NADPH.

Option 1 represents the requirement for a $C_{3}$ plant, which lacks the additional ATP cost for PEP regeneration.

Answer: 30 ATP and 12 NADPH

126301.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In most angiosperms, the development of a mature female gametophyte from a megaspore mother cell requires exactly one meiotic and three mitotic divisions.

Reason (R): The functional megaspore undergoes three successive mitotic divisions that are immediately followed by cell wall formation at each step to generate the mature embryo sac.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
126301.sol:
Assertion (A) is true: The development of a mature female gametophyte (embryo sac) from a diploid megaspore mother cell involves one meiotic division (to form four haploid megaspores, out of which one is functional) and three successive mitotic divisions of the functional megaspore.

Reason (R) is false: The mitotic divisions of the functional megaspore are strictly free-nuclear, meaning that nuclear divisions are not followed immediately by cell wall formation. It is only after the 8-nucleate stage is reached that cell walls are laid down to organize the typical 7-celled embryo sac.

Therefore, (A) is true but (R) is false.

Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false

126446.text: What are biomolecules commonly referred to as?
126446.sol: If one were to make a list of biomolecules, such a list would havethousands of organic compounds including amino acids, sugars, etc. For several reasons, we can call these biomolecules as ‘metabolites’. 127017.text: According to Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), which particulate size in diameter (in micrometres) of the air pollutants is responsible for greatest harm to human health?
127017.sol: Particles in the size range $1-10 \mu \mathrm{m}$ have measurable settling velocities but are readily stirred by air movements whereas particles of size 0.1-1 $\mu \mathrm{m}$ have small settling velocities. Those below $0.1 \mu \mathrm{m}$, a submicroscopic size found in Urban air, undergo random Brownian motion resulting from collisions among individual molecules. Of all the different types of particulates in the atmosphere, the presence of trace elements such as cadmium, lead, nickel and mercury may constitute the greatest health hazard.

127478.subject: Botany
127478.text: Which organization publishes the 'Red Data Book"?
127478.sol:
The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) maintains the Red Data Book. It is a public document which is created for recording endangered and rare species of plants, animals, fungi as well as some local subspecies which are present in a particular region. It helps us in providing complete information for rescarch, studies and also for monitoring the programs on rare and endangered species and their habitats.
Related Theory
Red Data Book of India includes the conservation status of animals and plants which are endemic to the Indian subcontinent. The data for this book is provided through surveys which are conducted by the Zoological Survey of India and the Botanical Survey of India under the guidance of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
! Caution
The red list contains only the names of the endangered species; however, the Red Data Book contains the information about the species that are on the verge of extinction.

127581.subject: Botany
options: The accumulation of a dark coloured amorphous substance
The process by which water:soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon
The process of breaking down detritus into inorganic substances
127581.sol: You may have heard of the earthworm being referred to as the farmer’s ‘friend’. This is so because they help in the breakdown of complex organic matter as well as in loosening of the soil. Similarly, decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances like carbon dioxide, water and nutrients and the process is called decomposition. Dead plant remains such as leaves, bark, flowers and dead remains of animals, including fecal matter, constitute detritus, which is the raw material for decomposition. The important steps in the process of decomposition are fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and mineralization .Detritivores (e.g., earthworm) break down detritus into smaller particles. This process is called fragmentation. By the process of leaching, water- soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts. Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances. This process is called as catabolism. It is important to note that all the above steps in decomposition operate simultaneously on the detritus Humification and mineralisation occur during decomposition in the soil. Humification leads to accumulation of a dark coloured amorphous substance called humus that is highly resistant to microbial action and undergoes decomposition at an extremely slow rate. Being colloidal in nature it serves as a reservoir of nutrients. The humus is further degraded by some microbes and release of inorganic nutrients occur by the process known as mineralisation.

127836.sol: Phosphorus is a major constituent of biological membranes, nucleic acids and cellular energy transfer systems. Many animals also need large quantities of this element to make shells, bones and teeth. The natural reservoir of phosphorus is rock, which contains phosphorus in the form of phosphates. When rocks are weathered, minute amounts of these phosphates dissolve in soil solution and are absorbed by the roots of the plants. Herbivores and other animals obtain this element from plants.
